We learned yesterday that a judge has allowed a $32 billion lawsuit to proceed alleging that the face recognition feature in Apple Photos violates state privacy laws.

While the two companies sit at completely opposite ends of the privacy spectrum, the case has repeatedly been conflated with Meta's use of face recognition. In allowing the case to proceed, the court fundamentally misunderstood how the feature works…

The earlier lawsuit against Meta

To properly understand this, we must first revisit a lawsuit over face recognition against Meta that dates back to 2015.

Because that facial recognition system ran on Meta's servers, and Meta could identify those faces, the company did indeed break the law and was rightly fined $650 million in a settlement.

Apple now faces a lawsuit under that same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which bars companies from collecting biometric data without consent.

Apple's approach is fundamentally different

There is a major problem with this allegation: Apple absolutely does not collect biometric data to power the face recognition feature in its Photos app. As Apple pointed out in a 2021 machine learning research paper, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

Beyond that, all your iPhone is doing is telling you "these photos all look like the same person" — it has no idea who that person is. The only person who can put a name to the face is the iPhone's user.

Apple's privacy policy for Photos reflects this same point.

What confuses me is that this lawsuit has been bouncing around the legal system for six years when a few minutes of research makes it abundantly clear the lawsuit's allegations are plainly wrong.

Courts and legislators should be actively praising Apple's approach to privacy rather than conflating it with the practices of privacy-destroying companies like Meta.

This is yet another example of courts and legislators failing to understand the technology they are trying to regulate. The most obvious example is, of course, end-to-end encryption. Multiple countries have threatened or attempted to ban end-to-end encryption, but they have no idea how encryption actually works.

I certainly understand that judges and politicians cannot be experts in every area. But they have access to experts, and what I cannot understand is how lawsuits and draft legislation can languish for years without anyone pointing out these fundamental errors.
